name: Mediterranean diet

lead: The Mediterranean diet is a plant-forward pattern built on olive oil, vegetables, fruit, whole grains, legumes, fish and nuts, with limited red meat and sweets. People use it as an everyday baseline for healthier skin and a leaner body.

The chain is unsaturated fats, fibre and polyphenols improving overall health markers and gut microbiota, with weight control as a flow-on effect. It is among the best-studied patterns: the PREDIMED trial and Lyon Diet Heart Study examined cardiovascular outcomes, and a Greek cohort linked adherence to survival. Direct trials on skin or looks were not identified.

paras: Meals centre on vegetables, legumes, fish, whole grains and extra-virgin olive oil, with moderate dairy and poultry and wine with meals in the traditional version. People adopt it as a long-term way of eating rather than a short cycle.
Cost and nutrient gaps outside the original cultural settings have been noted, and moderate wine is part of the traditional pattern.

angle.text: People use the Mediterranean pattern as a well-researched baseline for general health, skin and weight control, through olive oil, plants and fish improving overall health markers. Cardiovascular evidence is strong; appearance is inferred rather than directly studied.

lead: The Mediterranean diet is a traditional eating pattern of countries such as Greece, southern Italy and Spain. It emphasises vegetables, fruit, whole grains, legumes, nuts and extra-virgin olive oil, with moderate fish, poultry, eggs and dairy, low to moderate wine with meals, and limited red meat and sweets.[1] Researcher Ancel Keys popularised the idea after the Seven Countries Study.[1]

It is among the best-studied dietary patterns. Large cohort and trial evidence, including the PREDIMED trial in Spain and the Lyon Diet Heart Study, examined cardiovascular outcomes, and a Greek cohort linked adherence to survival.[2][3][4][5] Appearance communities cite it as an evidence-based alternative to fad diets for skin and general health; direct trials on skin or looks were not identified.
infobox: Olive oil, vegetables, legumes, fish, nuts

paras: Core features include abundant plant foods, olive oil as the main fat, fish two to three times a week, and limited red meat; the pattern is often shown as a pyramid with physical activity and shared meals at its base.[6][1] A 1995 paper described the Mediterranean diet pyramid as a cultural model for healthy eating.[6]

Early studies in the 1950s and 1960s in southern Italy and Crete contributed data; the Seven Countries Study was directed by Ancel Keys and published in 1970, and the Keys' publicized the diet from 1975.[1] UNESCO recognised the Mediterranean diet as intangible cultural heritage in 2010.[1]

The Lyon Diet Heart Study, a randomized secondary prevention trial, reported lower recurrence of cardiac events after myocardial infarction in people eating a Mediterranean-type diet, and an earlier trial examined an alpha-linolenic acid-rich Mediterranean diet in coronary heart disease.[5][7]

The PREDIMED trial in Spain randomized people at high cardiovascular risk to Mediterranean diets supplemented with olive oil or nuts, or to a control diet, and reported fewer major cardiovascular events in the Mediterranean groups, in 2013 and in a 2018 republished analysis.[3][4] A Greek cohort of 22,043 adults linked adherence to greater survival.[2] A trial compared weight loss with low-carbohydrate, Mediterranean and low-fat diets.[8] A study reported that high adherence changes gut microbiota and metabolome.[9] A 2019 Cochrane review is described by Wikipedia as finding modest cardiovascular benefits with low-to-moderate certainty.[1] No clinical studies on skin or facial appearance were found.
Grokipedia notes that confounding by lifestyle, cost of olive oil and nuts, and varying definitions limit generalisation outside Mediterranean countries; this is AI-generated and unverified.[10]
